title: Sausage, potatoes, and vegetables excluding carrots, broccoli, and dark-green leafy; gravy

content.title: About
content.content: A classic dish consisting of fried or boiled sausage, boiled potatoes and a mix of vegetables (e.g., bell pepper, onion, cauliflower) served with a thick gravy. Carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy vegetables are omitted, making it easier for those sensitive to those foods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sausage is often made from pork, beef or a blend, seasoned with herbs and spices.
Potatoes are one of the world’s most consumed tubers and are rich in starch.
Excluding carrots and broccoli is common for reducing bitterness and high vitamin K content.
Gravy can be based on stock, cream or tomato sauce, influencing flavor and calories.
The dish is popular at family meals and picnics because it is simple to prepare.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Sausage provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes contain potassium, which supports fluid balance and heart function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Sausage and some vegetables supply B1, B6 and B12 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Vegetables such as bell pepper and onion provide vitamin C and flavonoids that combat free radicals.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of carbs from potatoes and fats from sausage offers lasting satiety.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed sausages often contain a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: A significant amount of saturated fat in sausage may increase cholesterol levels.

items.title: Spice allergies
items.content: Some individuals may react to the spices or additives used in sausage.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is fairly calorie‑rich, so portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Glutamate content
items.content: Gravies made with ready‑made sauces can contain monosodium glutamate, which some people are sensitive to.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot: sliced sausage, boiled or baked potatoes and vegetables arranged on a plate, drizzled with gravy. Fresh herbs such as parsley or dill can be added for extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Store sausage and vegetables separately to prevent sogginess. Reheat thoroughly until the gravy is uniform.
